title: Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game
summary: One of the best ways to learn engine architecture is to read a real one. Many shipped games and engines have released their source. This lesson is a method for approaching a large, unfamiliar codebase: building it, finding the main loop, tracing one feature end to end, and recognising the patterns from this chapter in someone else's code.
markdown:
## Why read real code Everything in this chapter (the loop, time steps, entities, rendering, input, resources, saves, scripting) exists in every shipped game, solved under real constraints. Reading how experienced teams did it shows trade-offs no tutorial covers: what they simplified, what they optimised, which corners they cut to ship. ## Where to find source | Project | Notes | |---|---| | **id Software's games** (Doom, Quake, Quake III Arena) | Released under the GPL; small, clear C codebases, widely studied | | **OpenTTD**, **Wesnoth**, **SuperTuxKart**, **Cataclysm: DDA** | Large open-source games in C++, actively developed | | **Godot** | A complete open-source engine in C++ | | **raylib** | A small, very readable C library for games (used in the planned raylib course) | | **Dear ImGui** | The interface library of chapter 14, a famously readable single codebase | Respect each project's licence: reading and learning is always fine; reusing code in your own project means following the licence's terms. ## A method ### 1. Build and run it Clone the repository, follow its build instructions, and get it running under your debugger. A codebase you can run and step through is ten times easier to understand than one you can only read. Note what you had to install: the dependencies are a first map of the architecture. ### 2. Map the top level Look at the folder structure and the largest directories. Typical names: `engine`, `game`, `render`/`gfx`, `audio`/`snd`, `net`, `ui`, `script`, `tools`, `platform`/`sys`. Write a one-line guess for each and correct it later. ### 3. Find the main loop Search for the entry point (`main`, `WinMain`, `wWinMain`, or the platform layer's equivalent), then step into it with the debugger until you reach the loop that runs every frame. Note what it calls each frame and in which order: that is lesson 10.01's diagram for this engine. Quake III, for example, has `Com_Frame` doing exactly input, events, server frame, client frame and rendering. ### 4. Trace one feature end to end Pick something small and visible: what happens when the player presses fire, picks up an item or opens a door. Follow it from input to effect: ```mermaid flowchart LR I["Key press"] --> B["Binding / command"] B --> G["Game logic
(weapon fires)"] G --> E["Entity created
(projectile)"] E --> R["Rendered and
heard (sound)"] ``` Use the tools you have: search for the string on screen or in the console, set breakpoints, use the IDE's "find all references" (Shift+F12 in Visual Studio) and "go to definition" (F12), and the call stack at each breakpoint. ### 5. Look for the patterns As you go, match what you see with this chapter: | Look for | Lesson | |---|---| | Fixed or variable time step, and how `dt` is computed | 10.02 | | How game objects are stored: inheritance tree, components, arrays of structs | 10.03 | | Handles versus pointers between objects | 3.10 | | Where the renderer culls and batches | 10.04 | | Binding tables and action layers | 10.05 | | The resource cache and file formats | 10.06 | | Save code, and how it handles versions | 10.07 | | Data files and any scripting | 10.08 | ### 6. Write it down Keep notes as you go: a diagram of the main systems, the frame's order of calls, the path of your traced feature. Explaining the architecture in a page of your own words is the test of whether you understood it. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Reading files top to bottom > Large codebases are read by following execution, not alphabetically. > [!warning] Trying to understand everything > Pick one feature and follow it; the rest will become familiar along the way. > [!warning] Not running it > Reading without a debugger leaves you guessing which code actually runs. ## Knowledge check ```quiz ? What is the best first step with an unfamiliar game codebase? + Build it and run it under a debugger - Read every file in alphabetical order - Rewrite it in another language > Being able to step through it makes everything else faster. ? How do you find the code behind a visible feature? + Search for strings it shows, set breakpoints, and follow references and call stacks from there - Guess the file name - Read the main loop only > Follow execution from something you can see. ? Why trace one feature end to end? + It crosses most of the engine's major systems in a concrete, followable path - Because features are independent - To find bugs > Input, logic, entities, rendering and audio all appear along the way. ```
ideas:
- Clone the Quake III Arena source (released by id Software under the GPL), find `Com_Frame`, and write down what it calls each frame.
- Pick a game from the table, build it, and trace what happens when the player takes damage.
- Write a one-page architecture summary of the game you chose.

cards.q: What steps does the method follow?
cards.a: Build and run it, map the top-level folders, find the main loop, trace one feature end to end, match patterns to known ideas, and write it all down.

cards.q: How do you find the main loop?
cards.a: Start at the entry point and step through with the debugger, or search for it, until reaching the loop that runs once per frame.

cards.q: What should you check before reusing code from an open-source game?
cards.a: Its licence, and that your use follows the licence's terms.
